## How to use this handout

::: {.fiche n="0.2" etat="a-revoir"}
Intention : The shared user guide, plus what is specific to this course: the investigation, writing before the answer, the certainty bar, the revision mode. AI transparency statement. [new]
Experience : none
Request :
:::

This course is an **investigation**. Almost every slide asks you to look, write or choose **before** reading the answer.

- The **icon** in front of each title gives the level: **core**, to master; **support**, to consolidate; **further**, to go beyond. A slide without an icon is an example.
- The **writing boxes** keep what you write, in your browser only: you will find it again later on.
- The **certainty bar** asks you, before answering, how sure you are. At the end, the course compares your certainty with your results.
- The last part holds a **revision mode**, to reopen in a day, a week, a month.

::: {.transparence-ia profil="✒️ The equipped Author" coordonnees="F2 · R0 · S0" outil="Claude 5"}
:::

## Induction, deduction, abduction {.socle competences="C3"}

::: {.fiche n="1.3" etat="a-revoir"}
Intention : The cognitive process of the investigation. Marc's definitions: induction draws a rule from repeated facts (highly probable, never absolutely certain); deduction draws a conclusion from rules or premises (certain if they are true); abduction puts forward hypotheses to explain an observed fact (no certainty, leads, above all when the fact surprises). Sherlock Holmes's "deduction" is mostly abduction. [V0 feedback: Marc's definitions; the examples leave the boxes and form the bundle of clues, instead of shape / site / association / time; the multiple choice, which could be answered by reading, becomes a sort of three short reasonings on one example.]
Experience : diagram; sort three reasonings on one example
Request :
:::

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="60%"}
::: {.schema fichier="images/schemas/en/raisonnements.svg" hauteur="440"}
:::
:::
::: {.column width="40%"}
Three reasonings about one field. Which is which?

::: {.classer}
### Induction

- The hundred rapeseed fields seen in April were yellow: rapeseed flowers in April.

### Deduction

- Rapeseed flowers in April; the image is from April: its rapeseed fields are yellow.

### Abduction

- A bright yellow field in spring: perhaps rapeseed in flower.
:::
:::
::::

## Stating your certainty {.socle competences="C3"}

::: {.fiche n="1.6" etat="a-revoir"}
Intention : An interpretation without a degree of confidence is an opinion. Sherman Kent's "words of estimative probability" (CIA, 1964); the IPCC does the same in its reports. The exercise merges the student's certainty with the statement's: each sentence is completed with a word of certainty, on the image of the radio telescope, still unnamed. [V0 feedback: link with the IPCC scale; a single certainty, in the sentences, instead of two; four sentences suggested by Marc.]
Experience : sentences to complete with a word of certainty ("phrases" brick); bonus: the IPCC scale
Request :
:::

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="38%"}
In 1964, Sherman Kent, a CIA analyst, proposed matching words and odds:

| Word | Odds |
|---|---|
| Almost certain | about 9 in 10 |
| Probable | about 3 in 4 |
| Possible | about 1 in 2 |
| Unlikely | about 1 in 3 |

[A word of certainty commits you: it tells the reader what risk they take in believing you.]{.a-retenir}
:::
::: {.column width="62%"}
![](images/fast-2016.jpg){height="235" fig-alt="Satellite image of a large silver disc at the bottom of a wooded hollow, with blue-roofed buildings"}

::: {.phrases}
- It is {almost certain|=probable|possible|unlikely} that there are workers on the site : nobody can be seen, but the blue-roofed workers' camp is there.
- It is {=almost certain|=probable|possible|unlikely} that construction is under way : bare earthworks, new tracks, a workers' camp: the clues converge.
- It is {almost certain|probable|possible|=unlikely} that we are in the United States : these sugar-loaf hills and blue roofs rather point to southern China.
- It is {almost certain|probable|possible|=unlikely} that this image comes from an AI : the roads lead somewhere, the shadows are consistent.
:::
:::
::::

::: {.plus titre="The IPCC, too"}
IPCC reports describe the likelihood of an outcome with fixed terms, in italics in the text: *virtually certain* (99-100%), *very likely* (90-100%), *likely* (66-100%), *more likely than not* (over 50%), *about as likely as not* (33-66%), *unlikely* (0-33%), *very unlikely* (0-10%), *exceptionally unlikely* (0-1%). This terminology has been applied consistently since the Fifth Assessment Report (AR5).

[Source: Belgian federal climate portal, climat.be, "Rapports du GIEC" (in French).](https://climat.be/changements-climatiques/changements-observes/rapports-du-giec)
:::

**Which step of the method was missing?**
:::

## What is a forest? {.appui competences="C5"}

::: {.fiche n="2.3" etat="a-revoir"}
Intention : A nomenclature starts with definitions. Students build a definition of forest from three criteria (minimum area, tree height, cover), then find out whether such a definition exists: FAO, UNFCCC (Kyoto), BD Forêt V2, CORINE Land Cover, COMIFAC. Checked thresholds: FAO 0.5 ha, 5 m, 10%; UNFCCC, each country chooses between 0.05 and 1 ha, 2 and 5 m, 10 and 30%; BD Forêt V2 0.5 ha, 5 m, 20 m wide, aligned with FAO; CORINE 25 ha, over 5 m, at least 30%; COMIFAC (Ernst et al., 2010) 5 ha, 5 m, 70%. [V0 feedback: the nomenclature of the course image becomes the definition of forest, suggested by Marc: three series of items to combine.]
Experience : build a definition, then compare it with official definitions ("combiner" brick)
Request :
:::

Build **your** definition of a forest: one choice per row. Then see whether it exists.

::: {.combiner}
### Minimum area

- 0.05 ha [kyoto]
- 0.5 ha [fao, kyoto, bdforet]
- 5 ha [comifac]
- 25 ha [clc]

### Tree height

- 2 m [kyoto]
- 5 m [fao, kyoto, bdforet, clc, comifac]
- 15 m []

### Tree cover

- 10% [fao, kyoto, bdforet]
- 30% [kyoto, clc]
- 70% [comifac]

#### fao | FAO (world statistics)

Over 0.5 ha, trees over 5 m, a cover of over 10%.

#### kyoto | Climate (UNFCCC, Kyoto Protocol)

Each country chooses its thresholds within ranges: 0.05 to 1 ha, 2 to 5 m, 10 to 30% cover.

#### bdforet | BD Forêt V2 (IGN, France)

0.5 ha, trees over 5 m, at least 20 m wide; aligned with FAO.

#### clc | CORINE Land Cover

A minimum mapping unit of 25 ha; a forest has trees over 5 m and a cover of at least 30%.

#### comifac | Central African forests (COMIFAC)

At least 70% cover, trees of at least 5 m, a minimum mapping unit of 5 ha.

#### * | No known definition

None of the definitions kept here combines these three choices. Yet there are hundreds: every country, every database, every convention sets its own thresholds. A map of "the" forest always says **which** forest.
:::

## How accurate are experts? {.appui competences="C5 C6"}

::: {.fiche n="2.4" etat="a-revoir"}
Intention : One of Marc's slides on expert accuracy. It starts with "How certain are you of yourself?", voted with a slider: the expected answer is close to 95% (depending on age, progress in a field, tiredness, we do not always agree with ourselves: points developed orally). An expert is considered as such at 95%. Then four categories of accuracy in geographic information production, orders of magnitude given by Marc: expert photo interpreter 95%, expert classification highly variable, machine learning 80 to 85%, neural network 92%. The question on disagreements between interpreters stays. [V0 feedback: replaces "Two interpreters, two maps"; bonus: Colwell, 1952, on the links between military and forest photo interpretation.]

At **boundaries**, on **small objects**, on **cases the rules did not foresee**.

Military and forest photo interpreters have shared a lot: same keys, same methods. R. N. Colwell (US Naval Photographic Interpretation Center), "Relationships Between Military and Forest Photo Interpretation", *Journal of Forestry*, 50 (4), 1952, pp. 271-276. ## Data to teach machines {.appui competences="C6"}

::: {.fiche n="2.5" etat="a-revoir"}
Intention : AI learns from images labelled by people. FLAIR (Garioud, Gonthier, Landrieu, De Wit, Valette, Poupée, Giordano, Wattrelos, NeurIPS 2023): over 20 billion labelled pixels, 817 km² of 20 cm aerial imagery, with satellite time series. The interpreter becomes an annotator. Marc's reflection, kept here and not on the slide: AI takes in labelled data, not data being labelled; the interpreter's decision process is unknown. Including the margin of certainty in training data would be an interesting lead. [V0 feedback: AI learns the errors, not the hesitations; the orthophoto and its labels side by side.]
Experience : look at the image and its labels; question; bonus: the paper
Request :
:::

![](images/flair-ortho.png){height="215" fig-alt="Orthophoto of a small town surrounded by fields"} ![](images/flair-etiquettes.png){height="215" fig-alt="The same area, each pixel coloured by its land cover"}

[The image, and its pixel-by-pixel labels. The **FLAIR** dataset (IGN, 2023): over 20 billion labelled pixels, across 817 km² of 20 cm imagery.]{.legende}

::: {.question}
**Who makes these labels, and what does the machine learn from them?**
:::

::: {.reponse}
Interpreters, pixel by pixel, following rules. The machine learns their final decisions, **errors included**; their hesitations, it never sees.
:::

::: {.plus titre="The FLAIR paper"}
A. Garioud, N. Gonthier, L. Landrieu, A. De Wit, M. Valette, M. Poupée, S. Giordano, B. Wattrelos, "FLAIR: a Country-Scale Land Cover Semantic Segmentation Dataset From Multi-Source Optical Imagery", *NeurIPS 2023, Datasets and Benchmarks*. [The paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.13336) · [the data](https://ignf.github.io/FLAIR/)
:::

An AI maps buildings. Out of 100 random points, an interpreter checks: **90 are right**.

::: {.confiance}
::: {.qcm .serre}
What can be concluded?

- [ ] The map is 90% right, everywhere
    - No: errors may cluster somewhere (dark roofs, dense areas).
- [x] On this territory, about 9 points in 10 are right; we must look at where the errors are
    - Yes: the overall figure is not enough, the distribution of errors class by class is needed.
- [ ] The interpreter is no longer needed
    - No: the interpreter produced the check.

Intention : The step that deduces the dish's shape (Marc's request): 1. find where the sun is; 2. find a sundial (the tower at the bottom right of the disc and its shadow); 3. deduce the shape: the sun's reflection is on the side opposite the sun, so the dish is concave. On a dome, the reflection would be on the sun's side. The object is finally named: the FAST radio telescope. [V0 feedback: deduction step that was missing after the profile.]

- 46,59,13,8 : A sundial: the tower at the bottom right of the disc, and its thin shadow running left, across the disc.
- So the sun is on the right of the image, slightly low: opposite the shadow.
- 34,38,9,11 : The sun's reflection on the disc is up and to the left of the centre: on the side opposite the sun.
- On a bump, the reflection would be on the sun's side; in a hollow, it is on the opposite side.

The disc is **concave**: a hollow 500 m across, set at the bottom of a karst depression. It is the **FAST radio telescope** (Guizhou, China), the largest single-dish antenna in the world, caught by Pléiades on 2 March 2016, at the end of construction.

A reminder with images is planned (Marc's image to come). Bonus: OSINT and chronolocation. [V0 feedback: a reminder with images; link to OSINT and chronolocation; the image is no longer named.]

The date tells the **state** of a place: a construction site, a season, a tide, a time of day.

[Reminder with images to come (Marc's image).]{.legende}

::: {.confiance}
::: {.qcm .serre}
On the course image, the shadows of the buildings fall to the right (east). What do you make of it?

- [ ] The photo was taken in the morning
    - No: in the morning the sun is in the east and shadows fall to the west.
- [x] The photo was taken in the afternoon
    - Yes: the sun is in the west or south-west, shadows point east.
- [ ] Nothing can be said about the time
    - Yes it can: the direction of shadows gives the position of the sun.
:::
:::

::: {.plus titre="OSINT and chronolocation"}
**OSINT** (*open source intelligence*) is intelligence drawn from open sources: published images, videos, maps. **Chronolocation** is one of its branches: dating an image from its clues, the length and direction of shadows first. Tools such as [SunCalc](https://www.suncalc.org) give the sun's position for a place, a day, a time; the [Bellingcat](https://www.bellingcat.com) collective publishes its investigations and methods.
:::

## Reasoning step by step {.socle competences="C1 C3"}

::: {.fiche n="4.9" etat="a-revoir"}
Intention : A deduction tree on the Brest roadstead: what is happening inside the red dashes? Each choice is a clue; the path taken stays on screen, like a bundle. First version: the tree will be rebuilt from the answers of Marc's students, and its conclusions validated by him. [new]
Experience : deduction tree ("arbre" brick)
Request :
:::

What is happening inside the **red dashes**? Answer step by step: each answer is a clue.

::: {.arbre image="images/rade-de-brest.jpg" alt="Orthophoto of the Brest roadstead, a red dashed area on the water" style="--hauteur-arbre: 390px"}
### depart | How big are the small white dots? (scale: 200 m)
- A few metres → petits
- Several tens of metres → grands

### grands ! Measure again
With the scale, 200 m is about 126 pixels: a dot of 3 or 4 pixels measures a few metres. Go back one step.

### petits | How are they spread?
- Scattered, fairly evenly spaced → espaces
- Lined up in straight rows → rangees
- Packed in a group, all heading the same way → groupe

### espaces | Do they all point the same way?
- Yes, all the same way → mouillage
- No, at random → flottants

### mouillage ! Hypothesis: a mooring area
Boats on their moorings, all turned by the same current or wind, near the shore. To confirm: a slipway, a club, a harbour nearby? Conclusion to be validated.

### rangees ! Hypothesis: shellfish or seaweed farming
Buoys lined up on longlines. To confirm: sheds on shore, access tracks? Conclusion to be validated.

### groupe ! Hypothesis: a regatta
Sailing boats moving as a fleet. To confirm: wakes, a course mark? Conclusion to be validated.

### flottants ! Hypothesis: floating objects
Buoys, debris or birds. To confirm with a second date. Conclusion to be validated.
:::

An image captioned "Tiananmen, 1989, seen from a drone". **How many clues contradict it?**
:::

::: {.reponse}
- The **date**: in 1989, no drone films a protest like this.
- The **shapes**: tanks with inconsistent turrets and tracks.
- The **people**: figures with no proper shadow.

Three converging inconsistencies: the image is fake.

## What still gives AI away {.socle competences="C6 C2"}

::: {.fiche n="5.5" etat="a-revoir"}

Experience : look at the two images; list of weak points
Request :
:::

![](images/ia-textures-1.jpg){height="290" fig-alt="A dog licks a boy's cheek"} ![](images/ia-textures-2.jpg){height="290" fig-alt="A boy laughs, eyes screwed up"}

The weak points that remain, to look for with a magnifier:

- fine, disordered **textures**: fur, hair, wrinkles;
- **blurred backgrounds** whose blur does not follow distance;
- **fine details** (high frequencies), simplified into over-regular motifs: the signature of convolutional networks.

## The method {.socle competences="C6 C3"}

::: {.fiche n="5.8" etat="a-revoir"}
Intention : The verification method: source and provenance (metadata, content credentials), reverse image search, consistency with other images of the same place and day, converging clues. Never a single clue. [new]
Experience : put the steps in order
Request :
:::

::: {.ordre}
Put the verification of an image in order.

1. Where does it come from? Who published it, when, with what metadata?
2. Has it circulated before? (reverse image search)
3. Are the place and date consistent? (other images, the sun, the season)
4. Do the identification and interpretation keys hold? (shapes, textures, shadows, physics)
5. Conclude with a degree of certainty
:::

[No clue proves anything alone: a bundle, and a stated certainty.]{.a-retenir}

## Writing a note {.socle competences="C1 C3"}

::: {.fiche n="6.1" etat="a-revoir"}
Intention : The note in four headings (observations, interpretations, certainty, sources and limits), on the course image. The description written in 3.1 comes back. Link with "Cartography: Basics": clearly, honestly. [new]
Experience : the description comes back; the student writes the note, then compares it with the expert's ("observer" brick)
Request :
:::

An interpretation note has **four headings**: what I see; what I infer; how sure I am; on what sources, with what limits.

::: {.observer cle="note-image" rappel="description-image" invite="Observations… Interpretations… Certainty… Sources and limits…"}
**Observations.** A rocky coast, a breakwater enclosing a basin, two domes about 50 m across and a third under construction, long buildings, boils offshore, power lines.

**Interpretations.** A nuclear power plant by the sea, cooled by sea water (intake in the basin, outfall offshore), with a third reactor under construction.

**Certainty.** Almost certain for the power plant (a bundle of clues); probable for the water circuit (the tunnels cannot be seen).

**Sources and limits.** One orthophoto, one date; the outfall is inferred, not seen.
:::

::: {.column width="55%"}
Write your note on this radar image, with its four headings.

::: {.observer cle="note-baltimore" invite="Observations… Interpretations… Certainty… Sources and limits…"}
**Observations.** Quays, basins, a grid-pattern town; grey almost everywhere; colour patches on the water and on the quaysides.

**Interpretations.** The colours mark what changed between the dates: ships arriving or leaving, containers moved. Grey, what stayed put.

**Certainty.** Probable: we would need to know which colour matches which date.

**Sources and limits.** A radar image, whose source and dates are to be added.
:::
